keys.cAp: Secret for everything the browser sends after the handshake (the HTTP requests).
keys.cFin: The browser's proof, checked by the server.
keys.cHs: Secret for the browser's encrypted handshake messages.
keys.clientPub: The browser's X25519 public key, sent in the ClientHello.
keys.derived: A stepping stone that chains each stage to the previous one.
keys.early: The start of the schedule. Without a pre-shared key it is a fixed value.
keys.hs: Mixes in the shared secret: everything after ServerHello is protected by keys derived from this.
keys.iv: A 12-byte IV; each record's nonce is this IV XOR the record number.
keys.key: A 16-byte AES-128-GCM key derived from the traffic secret.
keys.master: The root of the application keys.
keys.sAp: Secret for everything the server sends after the handshake (the HTTP responses).
keys.sFin: Proves the server saw the same handshake. The browser recomputes and compares it.
keys.sHs: Secret for the server's encrypted handshake messages (EncryptedExtensions to Finished).
keys.serverPub: The server's X25519 public key, sent in the ServerHello.
keys.shared: Both sides compute this same value from their private key and the other's public key. It never travels on the wire.
keys.thSh: A hash of the messages so far, so the keys are bound to this exact conversation.
keys.unavailable: The real key schedule is only shown when TLS 1.3 runs with Web Crypto keys.

m.dns.arcount: {{n}} additional records, such as the name servers' addresses.
m.dns.class: IN: the Internet class, the only one in everyday use.
m.dns.counts: How many records follow in each section: {{qd}} question, {{an}} answer, {{ns}} authority, {{ar}} additional.
m.dns.flags.q: {{bits}}. An iterative question: tell me whatever you know.
m.dns.flags.q.rd: {{bits}}. RD = recursion desired: please do the whole lookup for me.
m.dns.flags.r: {{bits}}. Not authoritative: a pointer to someone who knows more.
m.dns.flags.r.aa: {{bits}}. AA = authoritative answer, straight from the zone's own server.
m.dns.flags.r.ra: {{bits}}. RA = recursion available: the resolver did the legwork.
m.dns.id.q: A random number. The answer must carry the same ID ({{id}}), which makes forged answers harder.
m.dns.id.r: Matches the question's ID ({{id}}), so the asker knows which question this answers.
m.dns.label: A length byte ({{len}}) followed by “{{text}}”. Names are labels, not dotted strings.
m.dns.name: {{name}}, stored as length-prefixed labels ending in a zero byte.
m.dns.nscount: {{n}} authority records: who is in charge of the next part of the name.
m.dns.pointer: Compression: instead of repeating “{{name}}”, point back to offset {{offset}}.
m.dns.rdlen: Length of the record data that follows.
m.dns.rootlabel: A zero-length label ends the name: the root of the DNS tree.
m.dns.rr.ar: Glue: {{name}} is at {{value}}, saving the resolver another lookup.
m.dns.ttl: Caches may keep this for {{ttl}} seconds ({{human}}).
m.dns.type: Record type {{type}} (A = IPv4 address, NS = name server).
m.eth.dst: The next device on this link: {{who}}. Wi-Fi carries the same addresses.
m.eth.src: The sender on this link: {{who}}. A locally administered address, not real hardware.
m.eth.type: 0x0800 means an IPv4 packet is inside.
m.h2.block: Headers. Real HTTP/2 compresses them with HPACK; shown here as plain text (simplified).
m.h2.preface: The fixed string every HTTP/2 client sends first.
m.h2.settings: Connection settings, such as how many streams may run at once.
m.h2.stream: Stream {{id}} carries {{resource}}. Many streams share one connection.
m.h2.type.data: DATA: a piece of a response body.
m.h2.type.headers: HEADERS: starts a request or a response.
m.http.end: An empty line ends the headers.
m.http.h.accept: Formats the browser is happy to receive.
m.http.h.age: Seconds this copy has been sitting in the cache.
m.http.h.cache-control: How long caches may reuse this response.
m.http.h.content-length: The body is {{value}} bytes, so the browser knows when it has it all.
m.http.h.host: Which site you want: one server can host many.
m.http.h.server: The software that produced the response.
m.http.h.user-agent: Who is asking: this simulator's browser.
m.http.h.x-cache: HIT: served from the CDN's cache. MISS: fetched from the origin.
m.ipv4.csum.bad: The checksum doesn't match: this header is corrupted.
m.ipv4.csum.ok: A checksum over the header. Verified ✓. Each router recomputes it after changing the TTL.
m.ipv4.df: Don't Fragment: if a link can't carry it whole, drop it instead of splitting it.
m.ipv4.id: Identifies this packet in case it ever has to be split into fragments.
m.ipv4.len: {{total}} bytes: a 20-byte IPv4 header plus {{payload}} bytes inside.
m.ipv4.ttl: Time to live: {{ttl}}. Every router subtracts one; at zero the packet is dropped, so loops can't go on forever.
m.ipv4.ttl.hops: It left at 64; {{hops}} routers each took one off on the way here.
m.ipv4.vihl: IP version 4, header length 20 bytes (no options).
m.port.ephemeral: Port {{port}}: a temporary port your laptop picked for this conversation.
m.tcp.ack: Acknowledges every byte before relative {{rel}}: “I have everything up to here.”
m.tcp.ack.unused: Unused: the ACK flag is not set yet.
m.tcp.csum.ok: A checksum over the segment and the IP addresses. Verified ✓.
m.tcp.flags.psh: PSH, ACK: hand this data to the application now.
m.tcp.flags.syn: SYN: let's talk. Here is my starting sequence number.
m.tcp.flags.synack: SYN, ACK: agreed. Here is mine, and I got yours.
m.tcp.off: The header is {{hlen}} bytes (20 plus options).
m.tcp.opt.mss: The largest payload I can take in one segment: {{value}} bytes.
m.tcp.opt.nop: Padding, so options line up on 4-byte boundaries.
m.tcp.opt.sack: Selective acknowledgment: these blocks arrived despite a gap.
m.tcp.opt.ws: Multiply my window by {{mult}}, so it can grow past 64 KB.
m.tcp.opts: Options. Here they only appear on SYN segments.
m.tcp.seq: Where this data sits in the byte stream (relative {{rel}}); {{len}} bytes follow.
m.tcp.seq.syn: The initial sequence number. It's random, so stray or forged segments don't fit.
m.tcp.win: I can take {{win}} more bytes before you have to wait for an ACK.
m.tls.ccs: A single byte, 1: encryption starts after this.
m.tls.cert: CN={{subject}}, issued by {{issuer}}, valid {{from}} → {{to}}, {{n}} bytes. A fake certificate made for this demo.
m.tls.chain: {{n}} certificates: the site's own first, then the issuer that vouches for it.
m.tls.ciphertext: {{n}} bytes of ciphertext ({{total}} in this record). Without the keys it looks like noise.
m.tls.comp: Compression is always off in modern TLS.
m.tls.cont.enc: Bytes {{from}}–{{to}} of the {{total}}-byte encrypted record “{{label}}”, which started in an earlier packet.
m.tls.cont.plain: Bytes {{from}}–{{to}} of {{total}} of “{{label}}”, continued from an earlier packet.
m.tls.ct.20: change_cipher_spec: a legacy signal that encryption starts now.
m.tls.ct.disguised: Says application_data, but in TLS 1.3 the real type is hidden inside the encryption.
m.tls.cv.alg: Signed with ECDSA on P-256 using SHA-256.
m.tls.cv.sig: A {{n}}-byte signature over the handshake so far (random bytes in this simulation).
m.tls.ext.0: Server Name Indication: {{host}}, sent in clear so the server can pick the right certificate.
m.tls.ext.0.ack: The server confirms it used the name you asked for.
m.tls.ext.10: Key-exchange groups the client supports: x25519.
m.tls.ext.13: Signature algorithms the client will accept.
m.tls.ext.16: ALPN: which protocol to speak inside: {{protocols}}.
m.tls.ext.23: Extended master secret, a TLS 1.2 hardening.
m.tls.ext.43: Supported versions: {{versions}}. This is where TLS 1.3 is really negotiated.
m.tls.ext.51: Key share: a public key sent up front, which is why TLS 1.3 needs only one round trip.
m.tls.exts: {{n}} extensions, where most modern negotiation happens.
m.tls.finished: {{n}} bytes that prove both sides saw the same handshake.
m.tls.frag: The first {{n}} of {{total}} bytes of “{{label}}”; the rest arrives in the next packet.
m.tls.hs.11: Certificate: the server's identity, vouched for by an issuer.
m.tls.hs.12: ServerKeyExchange: the server's signed key share (TLS 1.2).
m.tls.hs.14: ServerHelloDone: the server is done for now (TLS 1.2).
m.tls.hs.15: CertificateVerify: a signature proving the server holds the certificate's private key.
m.tls.hs.20: Finished: proves both sides saw exactly the same handshake.
m.tls.hs.8: EncryptedExtensions: settings sent after encryption starts.
m.tls.innertype: Inside the encryption, the real content type: {{type}}.
m.tls.legacyver: Claims TLS 1.2 for old middleboxes; the real version is in supported_versions.
m.tls.nonce12: The explicit nonce TLS 1.2 sends with every record.
m.tls.random: 32 random bytes, mixed into the keys.
m.tls.raw: Bytes that can't be parsed on their own here.
m.tls.recver: Always 0x0303 on the wire, for compatibility with old middleboxes.
m.tls.sid: A {{n}}-byte session ID, kept for compatibility.
m.tls.ske.curve: Key exchange on the x25519 curve.
m.tls.ske.sig: The server signs its key share with its certificate key.
m.tls.suite: A cipher suite: the encryption and hash to use.
m.tls.suites: {{n}} cipher suites the browser can use, best first.
m.tls.tag: The 16-byte authentication tag: any tampering makes decryption fail.
m.udp.csum.ok: A checksum over the datagram and the IP addresses. Verified ✓.
m.udp.len: {{len}} bytes: an 8-byte UDP header plus {{payload}} bytes of data.

story.ack: An acknowledgment: everything up to here arrived. TCP usually acknowledges every second segment.
story.ack3: Your laptop acknowledges the server's number: the connection is open, one round trip later.
story.cfin13: The browser checks the certificate and confirms with its own Finished: one round trip, keys agreed.
story.cflight12: The browser sends its key share and switches to encryption; a second round trip is needed.
story.ch: The browser offers cipher suites, names the site, and already sends a key share.
story.dns.1: Your computer asks its DNS resolver: what is the IP address of this name? Recursion desired.
story.dns.2: The resolver doesn't know either, so it starts at the top: a root server.
story.dns.3: The root doesn't know the address, but knows who runs .com, and says: ask them.
story.dns.4: The resolver asks the .com server the same question.
story.dns.5: The .com server points to the site's own name servers, with their addresses as glue.
story.dns.6: The resolver asks the site's authoritative name server.
story.dns.7: The authoritative answer: here is the address, keep it for an hour.
story.dns.8: The resolver hands the answer back to your computer and remembers it.
story.dns.8warm: The resolver already had this answer cached, so it replies right away.
story.dns.retry: ns1 stayed silent for 400 ms, so the resolver asks ns2 instead.
story.dupack: A segment arrived out of order, so the receiver repeats its last ACK to signal a gap.
story.fin: This side has nothing more to send and closes its half of the connection.
story.get.doc: The first HTTP request, encrypted: GET / for the page itself.
story.get.sub: The browser found {{paths}} in the HTML and asks for it on the same connection.
story.h2.get: HTTP/2 asks for {{paths}} at once, as separate streams on one connection.
story.h2.resp: Frames for {{paths}} come back interleaved on their streams.
story.origin.get: The CDN didn't have {{paths}}, so it asks the origin over a warm connection.
story.origin.resp: The origin sends {{paths}} back to the CDN, which will cache it.
story.resp.doc: The HTML arrives in encrypted records; the browser starts parsing right away.
story.resp.sub: {{paths}} comes back. With HTTP/1.1, each request waits for the previous one.
story.retx: TCP sends this data again because the first copy was lost.
story.sfin12: The server switches to encryption too and confirms. Two round trips in total.
story.sflight12: TLS 1.2: the server sends its hello, certificate and key share in the clear and waits.
story.sflight13: The server answers with its key share, then — already encrypted — its certificate, a signature and Finished.
story.syn: Your laptop asks to open a connection and picks a random starting sequence number.
story.synack: The server agrees, acknowledges your number and sends its own.
